title: METEORA: Rationale-Driven Retrieval for Safer RAG
one_liner: Generate an explicit rationale for what evidence is needed, use that rationale to select and stop retrieving adaptively, then use the same rationale to filter poisoned evidence before answer generation.
lead: Retrieval-augmented generation adds outside documents to a language model's context before it answers a question. In sensitive domains such as medicine, law, or policy, two extra demands appear: the system should be able to explain why each document was chosen, and it should resist poisoned documents that were inserted to mislead the model. Standard retrieval pipelines rank chunks by vector similarity and then keep the top k results, which gives little explanation for why those chunks were selected and little control over when retrieval should stop. This paper proposes METEORA, which turns retrieval into a rationale-driven selection process instead of a blind ranking step.

problem.h2: Similarity ranking does not explain evidence choice or defend against poisoning
paras: A standard RAG system embeds the query and all document chunks into vectors, ranks chunks by similarity, and keeps the top few. This is convenient, but the chosen cutoff is often arbitrary. Keeping five chunks rather than eight is a tuning decision, not a principled answer to the question of how much evidence is required.

The deeper problem is that similarity alone does not explain why a chunk is needed for the answer. A poisoned chunk can share vocabulary with the query and rank highly even if it contains misleading instructions or false evidence. In sensitive domains, a retrieval stage should articulate the evidence requirement first, then evaluate candidate chunks against that requirement, and finally reject chunks that satisfy similarity but violate the rationale.

callout.html: Similarity ranking can find related text, but it does not justify why each chunk is necessary and it gives poisoned chunks an easy way to enter the context.

panels.title: 1. Query enters a standard RAG system
panels.viz_args: query -> embed -> similarity search -> top k chunks
panels.caption: The system retrieves based mostly on nearest-neighbor scores.

panels.title: 2. Top-k cutoffs are arbitrary
panels.caption: A tiny score difference can decide whether evidence is kept or dropped.

panels.title: 3. Poisoned chunk can still rank highly
panels.viz_args: relevant words + misleading instruction = high similarity, bad evidence
panels.caption: Ranking alone cannot tell supportive evidence from harmful evidence.

panels.title: 4. METEORA writes an evidence rationale first
panels.viz_args: query -> rationale -> chunk pairing -> cutoff detection -> verification
panels.caption: The rationale defines what evidence is needed before any chunk is admitted.

panels.title: 5. Retrieval becomes selective and inspectable
panels.caption: The selected evidence is easier to justify and harder to poison.

steps.text: A preference-tuned language model writes what information is actually needed to answer the query safely and correctly.
Each retrieved chunk is evaluated against the rationale rather than against query similarity alone.
The system stops adding evidence when additional chunks no longer satisfy the rationale strongly enough, so k is chosen by content rather than by a fixed rule.
Chunks that conflict with the rationale or show poisoning patterns are filtered out before generation.

steps.b: Answer using the verified evidence set
steps.text: The generator receives a smaller, cleaner context whose selection can be explained to a human reviewer.

paras: The paper changes retrieval from ranking to selection. Ranking asks which chunks are nearest to the query. Selection asks which chunks satisfy an explicit evidence need and whether enough such chunks have already been found. That change also enables a verification stage, because the same rationale used for selection can test whether a candidate chunk is supportive, irrelevant, or adversarial.

hidden.h2: The hidden quantity: evidence necessity score
hidden.name: evidence necessity score
paras: The evidence necessity score is the hidden judgment of how much a chunk contributes to the rationale's information need. A chunk can be topically related yet unnecessary if it repeats what other chunks already provide or if it lacks the specific fact pattern the rationale asked for. Another chunk can be lower in raw similarity but necessary because it contains the decisive definition, citation, or contraindication.

METEORA estimates this necessity by pairing each candidate chunk with the generated rationale and scoring their match. Because the rationale describes the required evidence explicitly, the score reflects usefulness for the answer rather than raw lexical closeness. The cutoff detector then uses these scores to decide when the evidence set is complete enough to stop.

heat.caption: Dark cells mark chunks that directly satisfy the rationale's evidence need. Light cells mark chunks that may be similar to the query but do not deserve space in the final context.

reads.html: The system is asking a stricter question than similarity search asks: does this chunk earn its place in the evidence set? A chunk earns that place only if it provides needed support for the rationale.
Rationale-guided pairing turns retrieval into a query-specific evidence assessment problem, and the resulting necessity score supports both adaptive cutoff detection and poisoned-evidence filtering.

mechanism.h2: Why rationale-driven selection can improve safety and efficiency
paras: A rationale helps because it exposes the retrieval target before the documents are judged. Similarity search merges two questions into one score: is the chunk related to the query, and is it useful evidence for the answer? Those are not the same question. Writing the rationale first separates them.

Adaptive cutoff detection follows naturally. Once the system scores chunks by necessity, it can stop when the remaining candidates add little new support. That reduces context length because redundant or weakly relevant chunks no longer enter just because they happened to sit above a fixed top-k boundary.

The verification stage is the safety gain. Poisoned chunks often look relevant on the surface, but they fail a rationale-based check because they do not actually support the required evidence pattern or because they contain instructions and claims that conflict with already verified evidence. Reusing the rationale for verification creates a coherent retrieval policy instead of bolting on an unrelated filter.

stages.s: User query and a pool of candidate chunks
Generate an explicit rationale for the needed evidence
Score each chunk by how well it satisfies that rationale
Stop when enough necessary evidence has been collected
Verified evidence set for downstream generation

math.words: Each candidate chunk receives a score based on how well it satisfies the generated rationale. Retrieval continues while the next chunk still adds enough necessity score, and stops when additional chunks are no longer justified.
math.equation: select chunk c if Necessity( rationale, c ) > threshold;   stop when marginal_necessity(next_chunk) falls below cutoff
symbols: the explicit statement of what evidence is needed
the chunk's score for satisfying the rationale
the minimum score required for a chunk to enter the evidence set
how much new evidence value the next candidate would add
the stopping rule for adaptive retrieval

worked.title: A tiny worked example on a medical query
lines: Suppose the query asks whether a drug is contraindicated for patients with kidney impairment. The rationale says the system needs dosing guidance, contraindications, and severity thresholds.

Chunk A contains a dosing table and a contraindication statement, so its necessity score is high. Chunk B repeats background on the drug class without mentioning kidney impairment, so its necessity score is low even if it shares many topic words.

Chunk C contains an unrelated instruction that says to ignore previous safety guidance. It may be similar to the query, but verification rejects it because it conflicts with the rationale and verified evidence.
Retrieval stops after the system has enough high-scoring chunks to cover contraindication, dosage adjustment, and severity thresholds. Extra background is excluded.

math.note: The main point is that the stopping rule depends on evidence completeness, not on an arbitrary number of chunks.

bars.h2: What the method is trying to improve

charts.title: Similarity-ranked top-k retrieval
charts.note: The baseline spends context on related but unnecessary chunks and admits some poisoned chunks because similarity is not a safety test.

charts.title: Rationale-driven retrieval and verification
charts.note: Selection improves these metrics because each chunk must justify itself against an explicit evidence need before it reaches generation.

items.html: If the generated rationale misses an important subquestion, the retrieval stage can discard the chunk that would have answered it. Selection is only as sound as the rationale it starts from.

items.b: Verification inherits the same blind spot.
items.html: Because the verification stage reuses the rationale, a flawed rationale can reject good evidence or accept harmful evidence that fits the wrong requirement.

items.b: Candidate pool is already poisoned heavily.
items.html: If the upstream retrieval pool contains very few clean candidates, rationale-driven filtering may still struggle because there is not enough truthful evidence available to support the answer.

Train the rationale model on evidence-grounded preferences, keep candidate pools broad enough to contain clean support, and treat verification as a second-pass necessity check rather than as a replacement for source quality.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a small RAG benchmark with clean and poisoned document chunks for a sensitive-domain question set. Compare a vector-similarity top-k baseline against a rationale-driven pipeline that writes an evidence rationale, scores chunk necessity, stops adaptively, and filters conflicting chunks before answer generation. Measure evidence precision, number of chunks kept, answer accuracy, and attack success under poisoning.
demo.metric_eq: precision = relevant_selected_chunks / total_selected_chunks; attack_success = poisoned_answers / total_poisoned_queries
demo.closing: The demo should show that the rationale-driven system keeps fewer chunks while raising precision and lowering attack success because it selects evidence by necessity and checks each chunk against the same explicit requirement.
